task.query:
Has anyone applied cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks
(BOFN) with partial evaluations - i.e., an optimizer that models a multi-stage
pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models and chooses which
intermediate node (e.g., a cheap thermodynamic simulation or proxy experiment
vs. an expensive final property measurement) to evaluate next based on
information gained per unit cost - to an additive manufacturing pipeline for
metal alloys (composition -> powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion ->
microstructure -> mechanical property)? Consider both journal papers and
preprints, with emphasis on anything from 2025-2026, and include close
analogues (multi-stage / cascade BO, multi-fidelity BO with intermediate
process outputs, process-structure-property chained Gaussian processes) in
metals AM, alloy design, or other materials-manufacturing pipelines. Exclude
publications by Sterling G. Baird. State clearly whether the claim "applied
for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys"
is still defensible, and suggest a safer wording if not.
task.answer:
No. ## Assessment (literature searched through 6 October 2026)

**I did not find a non–Sterling G. Baird journal paper or preprint demonstrating the exact combination specified:** a cost-aware Bayesian optimizer that represents the *composition → powder atomization → laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) → microstructure → mechanical-property* route as a directed network of stage surrogates and adaptively decides whether to obtain another intermediate result or pay for a downstream measurement. This is a finding about the literature located, **not proof that no such publication exists**. Crucially, both the optimization method and nearly the entire physical alloy pipeline have substantial prior art; they should not be claimed as independently new. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12)

### Closest precedents and what they actually demonstrate

| Work | Demonstrated contribution | Boundary relative to the proposed claim |
|---|---|---|
| **Astudillo and Frazier, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks* (2021).** | Models a directed network with separate Gaussian processes (GPs) and uses expected improvement informed by intermediate outputs. | The original general-network algorithm evaluates the **whole network** at each iteration; observing internal outputs is not itself a partial-evaluation policy. (astudillo2021bayesianoptimizationof pages 1-2, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 2-3) |
| **Buathong *et al.*, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2023 preprint; ICML 2024).** | **Direct methodological precedent.** Its p-KGFN policy chooses a node and feasible input using expected improvement in the best posterior-mean solution **divided by that node’s evaluation cost**. In its principal setting, a downstream query uses *previously produced parent outputs*, so upstream dependencies are respected. | Its manufacturing example, **Manu-GP**, is a synthetic network sampled from GP priors, not an alloy-atomization/LPBF campaign; other demonstrations include molecular FreeSolv and pharmaceutical-product examples. Do not claim to invent cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 7-8, buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 8-9, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 9-11) |
| **Buathong and Frazier, *Fast Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2025 preprint).** | Accelerates node-level, cost-aware p-KGFN selection, reporting up to **16.03-fold** lower acquisition runtime. | Its **Manu** case remains a simulated manufacturing network. Unlike the earlier paper’s main feasible-input setting, this fast variant assumes a node can be queried at a feasible input **without first obtaining its parent outputs**; the authors identify physically constrained dependencies as future work. (buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 8-9, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 9-11) |
| **Torresi and Friederich, *Multi-stage Bayesian optimisation for dynamic decision-making in self-driving labs* (*Digital Discovery*, 2026).** | A particularly close **cascade-GP and partial-workflow** analogue: an inventory preserves intermediate samples; nested expected improvement chooses between starting samples and advancing existing ones. The framework permits stage-cost weighting. It is tested on synthetic cascades and retrospective molecular-property datasets, including simulated-versus-experimental hydration free energy. | **Not metal AM.** Moreover, although heterogeneous costs are tested, the authors report using **uniform stage costs in their principal experiments** because explicit cost weighting performed worse; their heterogeneous-cost benefit can arise from resumable sampling without putting cost into the acquisition. It should not be described unqualifiedly as an empirical demonstration of information-per-unit-cost selection in alloys. (torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 5-6, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 6-7, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 7-10, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 10-12) |
| **Taheri-Mousavi *et al.*, 2024 preprint and *Advanced Materials* article (2026), DOI 10.1002/adma.202509507.** | **Closest physical-pipeline precedent.** CALPHAD/ICME-informed **composition BO** led to a custom Al alloy; the authors screened compositions and printability, **ultrasonically atomized powder**, optimized LPBF settings, examined microstructure, and performed hardness and tensile testing. The journal abstract reports **395 MPa** tensile strength after aging. | Its BO selects alloy compositions against simulated design metrics; subsequent screening, powder production, printing and testing are **not reported as competing costed nodes selected by a BOFN partial-evaluation acquisition**. Thus the *integrated composition-to-property AM route* has precedent, even if the proposed **adaptive stage-selection rule applied across it** has not been located. (taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 7-9, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 1-4) |
| **Alvi *et al.*, *npj Computational Materials* (2026).** | Cost-aware, batch deep-GP BO chooses among **unequally costly property/information-source queries** for refractory high-entropy-alloy design; not every alloy receives every measurement. | The reported alloy case is **in silico** and concerns heterogeneous property tasks, **not sequential atomization → LPBF → microstructure → testing nodes**. (alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 14-16, alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 2-4, alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 1-2) |
| **Hur and Lee, *Compressing the Validation Bottleneck* (2026 preprint).** | Proposes a cost-aware metal-AM measurement agent that could use hardness instead of tensile testing, or X-ray/composition/CALPHAD instead of more expensive characterization, requesting the latter when prediction uncertainty is high. | Calls the DED-based metal-AM laboratory one the authors **“are building”** and describes evaluation in the future tense; it does **not establish a completed, experimentally demonstrated BOFN/LPBF pipeline**. It nevertheless makes broad claims about *first cost-aware intermediate-versus-final measurement decisions in metal AM* especially risky. (hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 1-2, hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 2-4) |
| **de Sousa *et al.*, *International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology* (2026); Comlek *et al.*, *Journal of Mechanical Design* (2025).** | De Sousa combines single-bead, single-layer and multilayer experiments with GP/multiobjective optimization for **AlSi10Mg laser directed-energy deposition**. Comlek fuses previously published **LPBF, electron-beam-melting and welding** data with a source-aware GP to predict Ti–6Al–4V yield strength. | Respectively, a staged **process-parameter** study rather than acquisition among costed pipeline nodes, and **predictive multi-source GP fusion** rather than sequential experimental BO. Neither is the specified LPBF alloy-production BOFN. (sousa2026gaussianprocessregression pages 1-2, sousa2026gaussianprocessregression pages 15-17, comlek2025heterogeneousmultisourcedata pages 13-17) |

Additional single-stage precedents are Tamura *et al.*’s 2021 BO of **Ni–Co superalloy gas-atomization parameters** and Kavas *et al.*’s 2025 preprint on BO-tuned **LPBF feedback control**. They optimize different parts of the proposed route, not a shared cost-aware, composition-to-mechanical-property function network. (tamura2021machinelearningdrivenoptimization pages 1-5, kavas2025insitucontrollerautotuning pages 1-3)

### Is “applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys” defensible?

**Not as written.** It leaves the distinguishing algorithmic feature unstated and can be read as claiming priority for applying BO to an integrated alloy-AM pipeline—despite the Taheri-Mousavi composition-to-powder-to-LPBF-to-property study—or for partial-evaluation, cost-aware network BO, which Buathong *et al.* had already developed. If the intended contribution is a *new application of an existing acquisition principle* to an experimentally realized, physically constrained **alloy LPBF process network**, a carefully delimited, qualified priority claim remains **plausible on the literature found**, but cannot be guaranteed by a search. It is important to specify whether intermediate queries are genuinely feasible given parent outputs and whether stage costs actually affect the next-evaluation decisions; merely recording intermediate observations, running inexpensive simulations before expensive tests, or using chained GPs is insufficient. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 6-7, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 8-9)

**Safer wording:** “To our knowledge, this is the first *demonstrated application of cost-aware Bayesian optimization of a partially evaluable function network* to an integrated **metal-alloy composition–powder-production–LPBF–microstructure–mechanical-property workflow**, in which the optimizer adaptively selects feasible intermediate or downstream evaluations under stage-dependent costs.” **Use “demonstrated” and list every stage only if the reported study actually executes or validates those stages and shows adaptive choices between them**; otherwise say “we propose a framework for…” and name only the stages implemented. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 2-4)

verbose.query:
Has anyone applied cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks
(BOFN) with partial evaluations - i.e., an optimizer that models a multi-stage
pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models and chooses which
intermediate node (e.g., a cheap thermodynamic simulation or proxy experiment
vs. an expensive final property measurement) to evaluate next based on
information gained per unit cost - to an additive manufacturing pipeline for
metal alloys (composition -> powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion ->
microstructure -> mechanical property)? Consider both journal papers and
preprints, with emphasis on anything from 2025-2026, and include close
analogues (multi-stage / cascade BO, multi-fidelity BO with intermediate
process outputs, process-structure-property chained Gaussian processes) in
metals AM, alloy design, or other materials-manufacturing pipelines. Exclude
publications by Sterling G. Baird. State clearly whether the claim "applied
for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys"
is still defensible, and suggest a safer wording if not.

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

filter for minimum publication year.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment

    ObservationalModel:

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Has anyone applied cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks
(BOFN) with partial evaluations - i.e., an optimizer that models a multi-stage

Abstract:
<jats:p>Gaussian processes (GPs) are a popular method in machine learning (ML) to model complex systems. One advantage of GPs over other ML models is their ability to quantify uncertainty in predictions. In the past, many advanced methods for GPs have been developed and published for various applications. Adaptive learning (ADL) is one of these applications, in which the consideration of uncertainty prediction plays a major role. The goal of ADL is to replace costly and time-consuming experiments and simulations of complex systems with surrogate models. This is achieved by strategically minimizing queries to maximize efficiency. In the ML literature, various reviews cover either GP methods or ADL strategies. Their focus is more on specific aspects. A comprehensive overview of different GP methods in various ADL applications was missing. This review categorizes GPs and related advanced methods for the first time in the context of ADL applications. A classification is provided for advanced GP methods, ADL methodologies, and practical application areas of GPs with ADL. This review distinguishes between ADL strategies with single-point and batch-query methods for Bayesian optimization and active learning, and highlights real-world applications such as material and product design, as well as efficient modeling for costly simulations and experiments. By combining these aspects, it offers a comprehensive guide for researchers and practitioners applying ADL with GPs to their specific use cases.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Hydrogen storage remains a central bottleneck for scalable hydrogen energy systems due to the multiscale and coupled nature of the thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural evolution of hydrogen storage materials (HSMs). Although artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated materials discovery, current approaches remain constrained by fragmented data, limited physical consistency, and weak integration with experimental validation. Here, we propose a unified framework that integrates coherent data infrastructure, physics-grounded modeling, and AI-driven inverse design within a closed-loop discovery paradigm. By constraining optimization with thermodynamics, kinetics, uncertainty, provenance, and experimental feedback, this approach enables adaptive, physically consistent optimization, thereby establishing a pathway toward autonomous, digital-twin-enabled discovery of HSMs.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Bayesian optimization due to its flexibility and sample efficiency has become a standard approach for simulation optimization. To reduce this problem, one can resort to cheaper surrogates of the objective function. Examples are ubiquitous, from protein engineering or material science to tuning machine learning algorithms, where one could use a subset of the full training set or even a smaller related dataset. Cheap information sources in the optimization scheme have been studied in the literature as the multi-fidelity optimization problem. Of course, cheaper sources may hold some promise toward tractability, but cheaper models offer an incomplete model inducing unknown bias and epistemic uncertainty. In this manuscript, we are concerned with the discrete case, where fx,wi is the value of the performance measure associated with the environmental condition wi and p(wi) represents the relevance of the condition wi (i.e., the probability of occurrence or the fraction of time this condition occurs). The main contribution of this paper is the proposal of a Gaussian-based framework, called augmented Gaussian process (AGP), based on sparsification, originally proposed for continuous functions and its generalization in this paper to stochastic optimization using different risk profiles for combinatorial optimization. The AGP leverages sample and cost-efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) of multiple information sources and supports a new acquisition function to select the new source–location pair considering the cost of the source and the (location-dependent) model discrepancy. An extensive set of computational results supports risk-aware optimization based on CVaR (conditional value-at-risk). Computational experiments confirm the actual performance of the MISO-AGP method and the hyperparameter optimization on benchmark functions and real-world problems.

Abstract:
Causal Bayesian optimisation (CaBO) combines causality with Bayesian optimisation (BO) and shows that there are situations where the optimal reward is not achievable if causal knowledge is ignored. While CaBO exploits causal relations to determine the set of controllable variables to intervene on, it does not exploit purely observational variables and marginalises them. We show that, in general, utilising a subset of observational variables as a context to choose the values of interventional variables leads to lower cumulative regrets. We propose a general framework of contextual causal Bayesian optimisation that efficiently searches through combinations of controlled and contextual variables, known as policy scopes, and identifies the one yielding the optimum. We highlight the difficulties arising from the application of the causal acquisition function currently used in CaBO to select the policy scope in contextual settings and propose a multi-armed bandits based selection mechanism. We analytically show that well-established methods, such as contextual BO (CoBO) or CaBO, are not able to achieve the optimum in some cases, and empirically show that the proposed method achieves sub-linear regret in various environments and under different configurations.

Abstract:
Multiobjective simulation optimization (MOSO) problems are optimization problems with multiple conflicting objectives, where evaluation of at least one of the objectives depends on a black-box numerical code or real-world experiment, which we refer to as a simulation. Whereas an extensive body of research is dedicated to developing new algorithms and methods for solving these and related problems, it is challenging and time-consuming to integrate these techniques into real-world production-ready solvers. This is partly because of the diversity and complexity of modern state-of-the-art MOSO algorithms and methods and partly because of the complexity and specificity of many real-world problems and their corresponding computing environments. The complexity of this problem is only compounded when introducing potentially complex and/or domain-specific surrogate-modeling techniques, problem formulations, design spaces, and data acquisition functions. This paper carefully surveys the current state of the art in MOSO algorithms, techniques, and solvers, as well as problem types and computational environments where MOSO is commonly applied. We then present several key challenges in the design of a parallel multiobjective simulation optimization framework (ParMOO) and how they have been addressed. Finally, we provide two case studies demonstrating how customized ParMOO solvers can be quickly built and deployed to solve real-world MOSO problems.                     We study black-box vector optimization with Gaussian process bandits, where there is an incomplete order relation on objective vectors described by a polyhedral convex cone. We also provide heuristic adaptations of VOGP for cases where the design space is continuous and where the Gaussian process model lacks access to the true kernel hyperparameters. This work opens a new frontier in sample-efficient multi-objective black-box optimization by incorporating preference structures while maintaining theoretical guarantees and practical efficiency.

This paper presents a novel AI framework with physics-informed features for fatigue life prediction of metals using three advanced models: LSBoost, XGBoost, and Deep Forest. A pivotal aspect is a domain-informed feature engineering methodology that transforms raw stress–strain data into 36 physically meaningful predictive features. These features capture key aspects of fatigue behavior, encompassing loading conditions, von Mises equivalent stress and strain, Goodman-corrected mean stress effects, detailed cycle characterization, energy-based damage measures, and indicators of multiaxial stress state. A dataset encompassing 25 material types and 589 experiments spanning both stress- and strain-controlled constant-amplitude multiaxial loading conditions was employed to train and evaluate a reliable AI framework capable of accurately characterizing fatigue behavior. Model hyperparameters are tuned using Bayesian optimization with a custom composite score balancing RMSE, MAE, R 2 , and generalization gap. XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy with a testing R 2 of 0.9357 (Pearson R = 0.9681) and RMSE of 0.2351 log₁₀ cycles, followed closely by LSBoost with a testing R 2 of 0.9225 (Pearson R = 0.9613) and RMSE of 0.2580 log₁₀ cycles, while Deep Forest yielded slightly lower predictive accuracy than the gradient boosting models. Permutation-based feature importance analysis identified equivalent-stress-to-UTS ratio as the dominant predictor by a substantial margin, followed by axial-shear phase difference, axial loading amplitude, and multiaxial Goodman safety factor, providing quantitative evidence that the proximity of the applied stress state to the material failure threshold and loading amplitude are the primary determinants of multiaxial fatigue life. This method relies on static parameter sets from extensive experimentation and simulations, hoping they remain stable and defect-free in production. Closed-loop control of LPBF can further enhance process stability and reduce defects despite complex thermal histories, process noise, hardware drift, and unexpected perturbations. Controller performance depends on parameter tuning, traditionally a manual, expertise-driven process with no guarantee of optimal performance and limited transferability between systems. This study proposes Bayesian Optimization (BO) to automate in-layer controller tuning by leveraging LPBF's layer-to-layer repetitive nature. Two approaches are introduced: online tuning, adjusting parameters iteratively during the process, and offline tuning, conducted in a setup such as laser exposures on a bare metal plate. These methods are experimentally implemented on an in-layer PI controller, and the performance is investigated on two wedge geometries prone to overheating. Results show that BO effectively tunes controllers using either method, significantly reducing overheating in controlled wedge specimens compared to uncontrolled ones. This study presents the first printed parts controlled by an in-layer controller subjected to microstructural analysis. Findings reveal partial presence of lack-of-fusion porosities due to insufficient laser power assigned by the controller, highlighting a significant challenge for utilizing laser power controllers. In summary, BO presents a promising method for automatic in-layer controller tuning in LPBF, enhancing control precision and mitigating overheating in production parts. Descriptor completion and cascade transfer for strength prediction in high strength steels Valid Text Names: 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 1-4', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 4-8', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 8-10', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 10-14', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 14-17', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 17-18', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 18-20', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 20-22', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 22-24', 'li2026descriptorcompletionand pages 24-25' BibTex: @article{li2026descriptorcompletionand, author = "Li, Hong and Wang, Wanlin and Dou, Kun and Okulov, Artem", title = "Descriptor completion and cascade transfer for strength prediction in high strength steels", year = "2026", journal = "Scientific Reports", month = "Sep", doi = "10.1038/s41598-026-69706-w", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-69706-w" } Abstract: Abstract

Accurate prediction of tensile strength (TS) and yield strength (YS) in high-strength steels (HSS) is hindered by incomplete microstructural reporting in literature-derived datasets, even though mechanical behaviour is governed by strong composition-process-structure-property coupling. Here, we develop a physics-informed machine-learning framework that distinguishes two routes for improving strength prediction under descriptor incompleteness: explicit microstructural descriptor completion and indirect TS-to-YS cascade transfer. Missing microstructural features were reconstructed using a hybrid scheme combining thermodynamic calculations, K-nearest-neighbour (KNN) estimation, and expert-guided scoring, yielding an enriched composition-process-microstructure (CPM) descriptor space in addition to a composition-process (CP) baseline. Direct and cascade prediction strategies were then evaluated under matched retained-feature budgets and repeated random train/test partitioning within a leakage-controlled workflow. Completed microstructural descriptors consistently entered compact retained subsets and produced generally favourable mean changes in direct HSS strength prediction across repeated partitions. The largest representative improvement was observed for YS under the compact 10-feature setting, where single-split test R² increased from 0.815 to 0.901, while repeated evaluation also indicated reduced between-partition variability in several key comparisons. Relevant Snippet:
We consider Bayesian optimization of the output of a network of functions, where each function takes as input the output of its parent nodes, and where the network takes significant time to evaluate. Such problems arise, for example, in reinforcement learning, engineering design, and manufacturing. While the standard Bayesian optimization approach observes only the final output, our approach delivers greater query efficiency by leveraging information that the former ignores: intermediate output within the network. This is achieved by modeling the nodes of the network using Gaussian processes and choosing the points to evaluate using, as our acquisition function, the expected improvement computed with respect to the implied posterior on the objective. Although the non-Gaussian nature of this posterior prevents computing our acquisition function in closed form, we show that it can be efficiently maximized via sample average approximation. In addition, we prove that our method is asymptotically consistent, meaning that it finds a globally optimal solution as the number of evaluations grows to infinity, thus generalizing previously known convergence results for the expected improvement. Notably, this holds even though our method might not evaluate the domain densely, instead leveraging problem structure to leave regions unexplored. Finally, we show that our approach dramatically outperforms standard Bayesian optimization methods in several synthetic and real-world problems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a transformative route for producing lightweight, high-precision, and geometrically complex components in aerospace, biomedical, and microelectronic sectors. Among AM technologies, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) offers exceptional design freedom; however, its widespread adoption particularly for titanium alloys remains constrained by two persistent challenges: shrinkage-induced dimensional deviation and porosity-related performance loss. In LPBF-processed Ti-6Al-4V, residual linear deviation typically falls within 0.1–0.8% when geometric compensation, preheating, and support strategies are implemented, while raw, uncompensated shrinkage is more commonly reported in the range of 1.2–2.0%, especially for thin-wall or thermally constrained geometries. Volumetric contraction (approximately 2–6%) may remain significant depending on part architecture and localized thermal accumulation. Concurrently, gas-induced and lack-of-fusion pores continue to undermine fatigue resistance and dimensional reliability. Research into process optimization, thermal management, and post-processing such as Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), vacuum sintering, and stress-relief annealing has improved density and mechanical integrity, while recent developments in AI-assisted monitoring, physics-informed models, and digital-twin frameworks are redefining defect prediction and control. Drawing on more than 100 peer-reviewed studies, this review synthesizes mechanism-driven insights and outlines a forward-looking roadmap, demonstrating how hybrid processing, real-time sensing, and data-centric control collectively advance the pathway toward defect-minimized, industrial-scale manufacturing of titanium components.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Bayesian optimization is a powerful framework for optimizing functions that are expensive or time-consuming to evaluate. Recent work has considered Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), where the objective function is given by a network of functions, each taking as input the output of previous nodes in the network as well as additional parameters. Leveraging this network structure has been shown to yield significant performance improvements. Existing BOFN algorithms for general-purpose networks evaluate the full network at each iteration. However, many real-world applications allow for evaluating nodes individually. To exploit this, we propose a novel knowledge gradient acquisition function that chooses which node and corresponding inputs to evaluate in a cost-aware manner, thereby reducing query costs by evaluating only on a part of the network at each step. We provide an efficient approach to optimizing our acquisition function and show that it outperforms existing BOFN methods and other benchmarks across several synthetic and real-world problems. Our acquisition function is the first to enable cost-aware optimization of a broad class of function networks.

Abstract:
Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN) is a framework for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate objective functions structured as networks, where some nodes'outputs serve as inputs for others. Many real-world applications, such as manufacturing and drug discovery, involve function networks with additional properties - nodes that can be evaluated independently and incur varying costs. A recent BOFN variant, p-KGFN, leverages this structure and enables cost-aware partial evaluations, selectively querying only a subset of nodes at each iteration. p-KGFN reduces the number of expensive objective function evaluations needed but has a large computational overhead: choosing where to evaluate requires optimizing a nested Monte Carlo-based acquisition function for each node in the network. To address this, we propose an accelerated p-KGFN algorithm that reduces computational overhead with only a modest loss in query efficiency. Key to our approach is generation of node-specific candidate inputs for each node in the network via one inexpensive global Monte Carlo simulation. Numerical experiments show that our method maintains competitive query efficiency while achieving up to a 16x speedup over the original p-KGFN algorithm.

Abstract:
Plastic injection molding is a fundamental manufacturing process used in various industries, accounting for approximately 30% of the global plastic product market. A significant challenge of this process lies in the need to employ sophisticated computational techniques to optimize the various phases. This review examines the optimization methodologies in injection molding, with a focus on integrating advanced modeling, surrogate models, and multi-objective optimization techniques to enhance efficiency, quality, and sustainability. Key phases such as plasticizing, filling, packing, cooling, and ejection are analyzed, each presenting unique optimization challenges. The review emphasizes the importance of cooling, which accounts for 50–80% of the cycle time, and examines innovative strategies, such as conformal cooling channels (CCCs), to enhance uniformity and minimize defects. Various computational tools, including Moldex3D and Autodesk Moldflow, are discussed due to their role in process simulation and optimization. Additionally, optimization algorithms such as evolutionary algorithms, simulated annealing, and multi-objective optimization methods are explored. The integration of surrogate models, such as Kriging, response surface methodology, and artificial neural networks, has shown promise in addressing computational cost challenges. Future directions emphasize the need for adaptive machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to optimize molds in real time, offering more innovative and sustainable manufacturing solutions. This review is a comprehensive guide for researchers and practitioners, bridging theoretical advancements with practical implementation in injection molding optimization.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Polymers play a pivotal role in advancing energy storage technologies because of their unique properties, including high conductivity, flexibility, and environmental stability. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into polymer science has revolutionized the design, discovery, and optimization of polymeric materials, enabling the development of faster, cost-effective, and innovative solutions. This review highlights the strengths of AI and ML, including their ability to handle complex datasets, optimize multiproperty trade-offs, and uncover hidden relationships between structure and properties. Future directions emphasize the development of sustainable polymers, generative design frameworks, and interdisciplinary collaboration to address pressing global challenges. By leveraging AI and ML, this work aims to accelerate the development of next-generation polymers for energy storage, fostering clean, efficient, and sustainable energy solutions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The generalization of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) used to solve the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation in a simplified three-dimensional room is investigated. PINNs are appealing since they can efficiently integrate a partial differential equation and experimental data by minimizing a loss function. However, a previous study experienced limitations in acoustics regarding the source term. A challenging but realistic excitation case is a confined (e.g., single-point) excitation area, yielding a smooth spatial wave field periodically with the wavelength. Compared to studies using smooth (unrealistic) sound excitation, the network’s generalization capabilities regarding a realistic sound excitation are addressed. Different methods like hyperparameter optimization, adaptive refinement, Fourier feature engineering, and locally adaptive activation functions with slope recovery are tested to tailor the PINN’s accuracy to an experimentally validated finite element analysis reference solution computed with openCFS. The hyperparameter study and optimization are conducted regarding the network depth and width, the learning rate, the used activation functions, and the deep learning backends (PyTorch 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.18.0 1, TensorFlow 2.18.0 2, JAX 0.4.39). A modified (feature-engineered) PINN architecture was designed using input feature engineering to include the dispersion relation of the wave in the neural network. For smoothly (unrealistic) distributed sources, it was shown that the standard PINNs and the feature-engineered PINN converge to the analytic solution, with a relative error of 0.28% and 2×10−4%, respectively. The locally adaptive activation functions with the slope lead to a relative error of 0.086% with a source sharpness of s=1 m. Similar relative errors were obtained for the case s=0.2 m using adaptive refinement. The feature-engineered PINN significantly outperformed the results of previous studies regarding accuracy. Furthermore, the trainable parameters were reduced to a fraction by Bayesian hyperparameter optimization (around 5%), and likewise, the training time (around 3%) was reduced compared to the standard PINN formulation. By narrowing this excitation towards a single point, the convergence rate and minimum errors obtained of all presented network architectures increased. The feature-engineered architecture yielded a one order of magnitude lower accuracy of 0.20% compared to 0.019% of the standard PINN formulation with a source sharpness of s=1 m. It outperformed the finite element analysis and the standard PINN in terms time needed to obtain the solution, needing 15 min and 30 s on an AMD Ryzen 7 Pro 8840HS CPU (AMD, Santa Clara, CA, USA) for the FEM, compared to about 20 min (standard PINN) and just under a minute of the feature-engineered PINN, both trained on a Tesla T4 GPU (NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA, USA).

Abstract:
<jats:p>The global drive towards net-zero has accelerated the adoption of carbon fibre reinforced polymers (CFRP) for lightweight structures in various sectors such as aerospace, automotive, energy and biomedical. Mechanical machining of CFRP is often necessary to meet dimensional or assembly-related requirements. However, significant challenges including surface defects (delamination, burr, surface roughness), rapid tool wear and material transition issues in drilling CFRP/metal stack, underscore the need for effective, automated process prediction / optimization for improved machining performance. Conventional physics-based models often fall short due to their reliance on extensive computational resources and inability to capture CFRP’s complex machining dynamics arising from thermo-mechanical load coupling and process uncertainties. To address these limitations, recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising, data-driven solutions that reduce reliance on domain-specific knowledge while delivering fast, accurate predictions by uncovering patterns within dataset. This provides a promising solution towards intelligent CFRP machining process with improved quality and efficiency. To date, there is a lack of comprehensive, up-to-date review of data-driven methods in CFRP machining process prediction/optimization. This review fills this gap and provides a critical analysis of data-driven methods in four key application settings: (i) machining process characteristics and surface quality/defects prediction; (ii) tool wear prediction; (iii) material transition recognition in CFRP/metal stacks machining; (iv) vision-based surface defects recognition. By presenting a state-of-the-art overview of advances, challenges and future research directions, this review highlights the transformative potential of data-driven methods in advancing intelligent CFRP machining within the manufacturing value chain.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The global transition toward sustainable energy has positioned multi-oil feedstocks (Garcinia gummi-gutta and Garcinia indica) to increase feedstock availability, which is vital to biodiesel production, thereby reducing fossil fuel dependencies and limiting harmful emissions. The incorporation of multifunctional CaO-Al
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    nanoparticles into biodiesel further enhances biodiesel combustion characteristics. However, predicting an engine performance (brake thermal efficiency: BTE, brake specific fuel consumption: BSFC) and emissions (carbon monoxide: CO, unburnt hydrocarbon: UHC, and nitrogen oxide: NOx) remains a critical bottleneck for currently practiced traditional and resource-intensive experimental methods due to complex interplay of fuel properties (biodiesel blends: B10, B20, B30, and nanoparticles concentration possessing an average particle size of 75.4 nm) and engine variables (engine load and compression ratio). To bridge this gap, this study used a CrayStack machine learning ensemble, which integrates three diverse base learners—Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Least Squares Boosting (LSBoost), and Support Vector Regression (SVR)—with a meta-learner whose ensemble weights are dynamically optimized via the cutting-edge Crayfish Optimization Algorithm (COA). This nature-inspired optimization method uniquely captures complex, multi-response nonlinearities using highly constrained experimental datasets (25 training, 10 testing), a task that conventional models fail to perform. In the CrayStack ensemble framework, COA evaluates the contributions of three base learners, with GPR having the highest contribution (> 50%) for BTE, BSFC, CO, and NOx, and LSBoost accounting for 52.3% for UHC. The Pairwise Wilcoxon single-ranked analysis confirmed that the CrayStack ensemble consistently outperformed SVR for all five responses. The CrayStack ensemble demonstrated superior predictive performance, with consistent results across all responses and the lowest composite Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 4.38%, outperforming GPR (4.93%), SVR (6.01%), and LSBoost (7.70%). Integrating CrayStack Ensemble with Monte Carlo simulations (MCS) yields probabilistic predictions that consistently outperform three base learner models, with the lowest error (RMSE of 0.35 and standard deviation of 0.02), ensuring robust and reliable predictions across all responses. CrayStack ensemble requires an average computational time of 3.736s, demonstrating its computational efficiency, robustness, and reliability for accurate engine performance and emission prediction applications. Thereby, CrayStack drastically eliminated experimental overhead (cost, power, materials) and provided a transformative, scalable tool to accelerate the commercial deployment of nanoparticle-enhanced sustainable biofuel blends.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 8-9'.

Poompol Buathong and Peter I. Frazier. Fast bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations. ArXiv, Jun 2506. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456. This article has 0 citations.

This excerpt describes the 2506.11456 Fast p-KGFN paper and its relationship to the earlier p-KGFN framework. The modeled action is an independent query to a selected network node at a feasible input, rather than necessarily executing a physically feasible upstream-to-downstream sequence whose parent outputs must first be available. Both methods support partial evaluations, and the fast method uses a cost-aware selection rule to choose the node and candidate input. Its computational shortcut generates one network-wide EIFN candidate, combines it with simulated intermediate surrogate outputs to form node-specific candidates, and then selects the action by cost awareness. Experiments cover the AckMat, FreeSolv, and Manu test problems; this excerpt does not identify an alloy additive-manufacturing application. The fast method has optimization performance close to p-KGFN, but p-KGFN is generally strongest because it fully optimizes its acquisition function. The reported computational improvement is as high as 16.03×, described in the conclusion as exceeding 16×. A key caveat relevant to novelty or scope is the assumption that intermediate nodes may be evaluated independently without parent outputs; the authors identify handling upstream-downstream dependencies as future work. The excerpt does not provide the earlier paper’s publication venue/date or establish a novelty comparison beyond these claims.

The excerpt supports the characterization of Fast p-KGFN as selecting an individual node and input for evaluation: p-KGFN candidates consist of nodes and input values, and the node with the highest acquisition value is evaluated, after which that partial observation is added to the dataset. It does not describe executing a physically feasible upstream sequence as the action. The method uses a cost-sensitive p-KGFN acquisition framework, although the excerpt does not provide the acquisition-function derivation; it does show explicit cost scenarios and comparisons against p-KGFN, EIFN, KG, EI, TSFN, and random search. Experiments cover AckMat, FreeSolv, and Manu, representing cascade/multistage or inventory-style problems, molecular/materials design with computational prescreening, and manufacturing processes. No alloy additive-manufacturing application appears in this excerpt. Runtime results report Fast p-KGFN speedups over p-KGFN from 4.24× to 16.03× across the listed scenarios, including 5.57× for Manu. The excerpt does not provide the first paper’s arXiv publication date or venue, nor does it state a novelty caveat; those points require additional source material.

URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146. This article has 15 citations.

The excerpt describes Buathong et al.’s November 2023 arXiv paper (arXiv:2311.02146) as introducing Bayesian optimization for general function networks with partial evaluations. The action is formally a node-level query: at each iteration the algorithm selects a node k and an input z_k at which that node function is evaluated. However, under the primary feasible-input setting, this is not an arbitrary independent node query: evaluating node k requires first obtaining the outputs of its parent nodes, so the physically feasible process follows the upstream dependency requirements. The proposed p-KGFN acquisition is knowledge-gradient based and cost aware. It values the benefit of one additional partial evaluation at a chosen node and input after normalizing that benefit by the associated evaluation cost; the objective is to improve the final node value while minimizing cumulative cost. The excerpt says the work includes synthetic and real-world experiments with varied network structures, but does not identify the application domains, any alloy additive-manufacturing application, computational speedup, or publication venue. It also does not provide details about the later arXiv:2506.11456 paper, so no comparison with that work or verification of its claims is supported here. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146. This article has 15 citations.

The excerpt describes p-KGFN as an action that selects a node k and an input z_k for one partial evaluation, rather than selecting x and physically evaluating the entire network as the comparison algorithms do. It contrasts p-KGFN with KGFN: both are one-step lookahead policies, but KGFN assumes full function-network evaluations while p-KGFN obtains one additional observation at a single node. The inner acquisition optimization is decomposable across previously evaluated fantasies and nodes, so each node-specific optimization can be solved independently and in parallel; with sufficient parallel resources, its wall-time complexity is equivalent to solving a single-node problem from one starting point. The experiments compare p-KGFN with Random, EI, KG, EIFN, KGFN, and TSFN, using synthetic sequential and multiprocess/multi-output networks plus real-world applications, including materials-design and manufacturing-motivated settings. The excerpt gives examples such as Ackley6D and Manu-GP, and emphasizes cheaper upstream versus expensive downstream evaluations. It does not provide the requested publication venue/date, the later 2025 paper’s details, an alloy additive-manufacturing application, a numerical computational speedup, or a broader novelty caveat beyond stating that KGFN had not previously been proposed and that this work was the first to describe KG policies for function networks with partial and full evaluations.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 2-4'.

Poompol Buathong and Peter I. Frazier. Fast bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations. ArXiv, Jun 2506. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt describes Fast Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations (arXiv:2506.11456) as operating through independent, node-level partial evaluations: at each iteration it constructs a candidate input for every node, evaluates the p-KGFN acquisition value, selects the node with the largest value, performs that single node evaluation, updates that node’s GP, and charges its node-specific cost. The p-KGFN acquisition is explicitly cost-aware: it measures expected improvement in the best posterior-mean network solution divided by the evaluation cost. The fast method uses a discrete candidate set and adds novel batch-Thompson-sampling and local-point methods, while also using an EIFN candidate and sampled GP realizations. The excerpt explicitly distinguishes this setting from an application restriction requiring upstream parent evaluations first; the authors state that they do not impose that restriction and assume a node can be evaluated at any input in a known set containing possible parent outputs. It reports comparable optimization results and significant acceleration relative to original p-KGFN, but the supplied pages do not give a numerical speedup. They also contain no experiment/application-domain details, no alloy additive-manufacturing example, and no explicit caveat about novelty beyond noting that the approach may be extended to settings with upstream-feasibility restrictions.

The excerpt describes Buathong et al. (arXiv:2311.02146) as a Bayesian-optimization method for function networks in which evaluations may be partial rather than full-network. Its action is to select an individual node and a corresponding input for evaluation, then use the resulting information to choose inputs to subsequent nodes; the introduction explicitly contrasts this with evaluating the full network at every iteration. The proposed p-KGFN is a knowledge-gradient acquisition function that chooses the node and inputs in a cost-aware way, with the goal of reducing query costs when node evaluation costs differ. The motivating example is that a cheap upstream node can be evaluated to learn its output range before undertaking expensive downstream evaluations. The excerpt lists manufacturing, epidemic-model calibration, machine-learning pipeline optimization, and robotic control as application domains, and says experiments cover synthetic and real-world problems. It claims the acquisition function is the first to enable cost-aware optimization of a broad class of function networks, but this is a novelty claim from the paper rather than an independently established fact. The supplied pages do not provide the publication venue/date beyond the November 2023 arXiv citation, do not describe arXiv:2506.11456 or a physically feasible upstream-sequence action, and do not report a computational speedup or an alloy-additive-manufacturing application.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 9-10'.

Poompol Buathong, Jiayue Wan, Raul Astudillo, Samuel Daulton, Maximilian Balandat, and Peter I. Frazier. Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations. ArXiv, Nov 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2311.02146. This article has 15 citations.

The excerpt describes p-KGFN as a cost-aware, knowledge-gradient approach that can select partial evaluations rather than requiring every baseline to perform full function-network evaluations. In the reported two-node examples, it often evaluates the upstream/first function node thoroughly and only evaluates the downstream/second node in regions with high potential, especially when the downstream node is more expensive. When node costs are equal, it generally behaves more like full evaluation; the benefits of partial evaluation increase as downstream cost rises. The method is reported to outperform the baselines across the experiments, with gains especially strong when downstream nodes are highly correlated with their parents and costly to evaluate. Experiments include synthetic and real-world settings such as Ackley and FreeSolv, and cover sequential, multi-process, and multi-output networks. The excerpt does not provide the requested publication venue/date comparison with arXiv:2506.11456, any alloy additive-manufacturing application, a numerical computational-speedup figure, or a caveat concerning the work’s novelty. It does note an important computational tradeoff: optimizing p-KGFN’s acquisition function can be expensive because it considers all nodes and available outputs, and the method uses only single-step lookahead.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 1-2'.

Poompol Buathong and Peter I. Frazier. Fast bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations. ArXiv, Jun 2506. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt describes the 2025 Buathong–Frazier Fast p-KGFN work, but does not provide the bibliographic publication venue/date details for the earlier arXiv:2311.02146 paper, nor any alloy-additive-manufacturing experiment. It characterizes function-network optimization using a DAG of constituent functions and explains that partial evaluations query only selected nodes rather than necessarily evaluating the entire objective. The earlier p-KGFN method chooses nodes and inputs using a knowledge-gradient acquisition function that values information per unit evaluation cost, thereby reducing expensive objective evaluations; however, its acquisition computation requires nested Monte Carlo optimization over a mixed discrete/continuous space. Fast p-KGFN addresses this computational bottleneck by generating node-specific candidate inputs through one inexpensive global Monte Carlo simulation and rapidly evaluating the acquisition function on those candidates, avoiding the original nested optimization. The reported result is competitive query/optimization efficiency with substantially lower computational overhead, including up to a 16-fold speedup. The excerpt also frames the method as an accelerated approach that retains much of p-KGFN’s benefit with a modest loss in query efficiency. It does not establish whether the underlying action should be interpreted as an independently executable node query or as a physically feasible upstream sequence, and it contains no explicit novelty caveat beyond describing the proposed candidate-generation and fast-evaluation approach as novel.
