Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a transformative technology for producing complex geometries with tailored mechanical properties. However, achieving optimal part quality and performance requires precise control over processing parameters such as laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, and hatch spacing. This study presents an analytical framework for predicting optimized processing parameters in metal AM, focusing on the interplay between thermal dynamics, microstructure evolution, and mechanical properties. The proposed approach integrates thermal modeling, solidification kinetics, and machine learning algorithms to identify optimized parameter sets that maximize mechanical strength. The framework is validated through experimental data from laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of titanium alloys, demonstrating its capability to predict parameter combinations that yield superior part quality. This work provides a systematic pathway for accelerating the development of optimized metal AM processes, reducing trial-and-error experimentation, and enhancing the reliability of AM-produced components.

Efficient exploration of vast compositional and processing spaces is essential for accelerated materials discovery. Bayesian optimization (BO) provides a principled strategy for identifying optimal materials with minimal experiments, yet its adoption in materials science ishindered by implementation complexity and limited domain-specific tools. Here, we presentBgolearn, a comprehensive Python framework that makes BO accessible and practical for materials research through an intuitive interface, robust algorithms, and materials-oriented workflows. Bgolearn supports both single-objective and multi-objective Bayesian optimization withmultiple acquisition functions (e.g., expected improvement, upper confidence bound, probability of improvement, and expected hypervolume improvement etc.), diverse surrogate models(including Gaussian processes, random forests, and gradient boosting etc.), and bootstrapbased uncertainty quantification. Benchmark studies show that Bgolearn reduces the numberof required experiments by 40–60% compared with random search, grid search, and geneticalgorithms, while maintaining comparable or superior solution quality. Its effectiveness isdemonstrated not only through the studies presented in this paper, such as the identificationof maximum-elastic-modulus triply periodic minimal surface structures, ultra-high-hardnesshigh-entropy alloys, and high-strength, high-ductility medium-Mn steels, but also by numerous publications that have proven its impact in material discovery. With a modular architecture that integrates seamlessly into existing materials workflows and a graphical user interface (BgoFace) that removes programming barriers, Bgolearn establishes a practical andreliable platform for Bayesian optimization in materials science, and is openly available athttps://github.com/Bin-Cao/Bgolearn.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 Tailoring materials to achieve a desired behavior in specific applications is of significant scientific and industrial interest as design of materials is a key driver to innovation. Overcoming the rather slow and expertise-bound traditional forward approaches of trial and error, inverse design is attracting substantial attention. Targeting a property, the design model proposes a candidate structure with the desired property. This concept can be particularly well applied to the field of architected materials as their structures can be directly tuned. The bone-like spinodoid materials are a specific class of architected materials. They are of considerable interest thanks to their non-periodicity, smoothness, and low-dimensional statistical description. Previous work successfully employed machine learning (ML) models for inverse design. The amount of data necessary for most ML approaches poses a severe obstacle for broader application, especially in the context of inelasticity. That is why we propose an inverse-design approach based on Bayesian optimization to operate in the small-data regime. Necessitating substantially less data, a small initial data set is iteratively augmented by in silico generated data until a structure with the targeted properties is found. The application to the inverse design of spinodoid structures of desired elastic properties demonstrates the framework’s potential for paving the way for advance in inverse design.

Abstract:

 Artificial intelligence and machine learning frameworks have become powerful tools for establishing computationally efficient mappings between inputs and outputs in engineering problems. These mappings have enabled optimization and analysis routines, leading to innovative designs, advanced material systems, and optimized manufacturing processes. In such modeling efforts, it is common to encounter multiple information (data) sources, each varying in specifications. Data fusion frameworks offer the capability to integrate these diverse sources into unified models, enhancing predictive accuracy and enabling knowledge transfer. However, challenges arise when these sources are heterogeneous, i.e., they do not share the same input parameter space. Such scenarios occur when domains differentiated by complexity such as fidelity, operating conditions, experimental setup, and scale, require distinct parametrizations. To address this challenge, a heterogeneous multi-source data fusion framework based on input mapping calibration (IMC) and latent variable Gaussian process (LVGP) is proposed. In the first stage, the IMC algorithm transforms the heterogeneous input parameter spaces into a unified reference parameter space. In the second stage, an LVGP-enabled multi-source data fusion model constructs a single source-aware surrogate model on the unified space. The framework is demonstrated and analyzed through three engineering case studies: the design of a cantilever beam, the design of ellipsoidal voids, and the modeling of Ti6Al4V alloy properties. The results demonstrate that the framework achieves higher predictive accuracy compared to both single-source models and source-unaware models on the transformed space.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Due to its unique benefits over conventional subtractive manufacturing, additive manufacturing methods continue to attract interest in both academia and industry. One such method is called Cold Spray Additive Manufacturing (CSAM), a solid-state coating deposition technology to manufacture repair metallic components using a gas jet and powder particles. CSAM offers low heat input, stable phases, suitability for heat-sensitive substrates, and high deposition rates. However, persistent challenges include porosity control, geometric accuracy near edges and concavities, anisotropy, and cost sensitivities linked to gas selection and nozzle wear. Interdisciplinary research across manufacturing science, materials characterisation, robotics, control, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) is deployed to overcome these issues. ML supports quality prediction, inverse parameter design, in situ monitoring, and surrogate models that couple process physics with data. To demonstrate the impact of AI and ML on CSAM, this study presents a systematic literature review to identify, evaluate, and analyse published studies in this domain. The most relevant studies in the literature are analysed using keyword co-occurrence and clustering. Four themes were identified: design for CSAM, material analytics, real-time monitoring and defect analytics, and deposition and AI-enabled optimisation. Based on this synthesis, core challenges are identified as small and varied datasets, transfer and identifiability limits, and fragmented sensing. Main opportunities are outlined as physics-based surrogates, active learning, uncertainty-aware inversion, and cloud-edge control for reliable and adaptable ML use in CSAM. By systematically mapping the current landscape, this work provides a critical roadmap for researchers to target the most significant challenges and opportunities in applying AI/ML to industrialise CSAM.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000028

Sk Md Ahnaf Akif Alvi, Brent Vela, V. Attari, Jan Janssen, Danny Perez, Douglas L. Allaire, and Raymundo Arróyave. Deep gaussian process-based cost-aware batch bayesian optimization for complex materials design campaigns. npj Computational Materials, Feb 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-026-01981-7, doi:10.1038/s41524-026-01981-7. This article has 7 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Alvi et al. present a cost-aware, batch heterotopic deep Gaussian process Bayesian optimization framework for multi-objective materials discovery. The approach allocates queries across property-evaluation tasks with unequal costs: expensive properties such as thermal conductivity and solidus temperature receive relatively few evaluations, while cheaper measurements—including density, Pugh ratio, hardness, and BCC phase fraction—are sampled more heavily. These are partial or auxiliary property measurements rather than intermediate manufacturing-process states; the model uses learned inter-task correlations so abundant inexpensive data can improve predictions for expensive properties. The demonstrated materials case is a seven-dimensional Ti–Ta–V–W–Cr–Fe–Hf refractory high-entropy-alloy composition space, optimizing solidus temperature, thermal conductivity, yield strength, BCC phase fraction, and density. The study is explicitly an in-silico CALPHAD-based campaign, not an experimental alloy metal-additive-manufacturing deployment. The authors identify future joint chemistry–process optimization—such as temperature profiles, cooling rates, mechanical working parameters, and synthesis routes—as a needed extension. Thus, this excerpt supports classification as cost-aware and multi-task/heterotopic, but does not document an actually applied additive-manufacturing DAG or an experimental process DAG.

Chawla et al. present a cost-aware, high-throughput materials-discovery workflow based on random combinatorial libraries and automated nanoindentation. A single specimen contains hundreds to thousands of microscale particles, each representing a distinct composition or composition-space point. EDS is used first to localize and map chemistry, after which automated nanoindentation supplies localized mechanical-property measurements. Thus, the workflow uses partial/intermediate measurements in the sense that chemical localization and instrument constraints inform which indentation sites are selected; it is not merely a collection of independent black-box tasks. The planning layer uses Gaussian-process surrogate modeling and cost-aware experimental planning, accounting for stage motion, reconfiguration overhead, positional accuracy, EDS noise/resolution, and minimum particle sizes. The excerpt frames this as an instrument-agnostic route for structural-materials discovery and demonstrates a particle-based library experimentally. However, these pages do not describe a metal additive-manufacturing process, an applied alloy such as Ti6Al4V, or a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing additive-manufacturing tasks. Kyunghoon Hur and Chi-Hun Lee. Compressing the validation bottleneck: an agentic self-driving lab for scientific discovery. ArXiv, Jul 2607. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.04508, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2607.04508. This article has 0 citations.

The Hur and Lee excerpt describes two distinct validation bottlenecks addressed by one agent. The first is an agentic DOE loop intended to reduce the number of experimental rounds by combining domain knowledge, literature priors, past results, and bench-side feasibility constraints before proposing the next experiment. The second is explicitly cost-aware: a surrogate agent predicts expensive, high-resolution measurements from cheaper, lower-resolution measurements and decides whether to rely on the surrogate or request the expensive measurement according to predicted uncertainty. The stated examples are hardness-to-tensile-strength prediction and prediction of phase fraction from X-ray measurements combined with composition and CALPHAD information in metal additive manufacturing. Thus, the work concerns partial or intermediate measurement substitution rather than merely assigning costs to whole experimental tasks. The excerpt frames the metal additive-manufacturing setting as “the lab we are building,” so it does not establish that a fully deployed, experimentally applied alloy-metal-AM DAG already exists. It also does not provide details about the other cited 2026 competitors, their implementations, or comparative results.

The excerpt directly supports classifying Alvi et al. as cost-aware: evaluation cost is explicitly incorporated into an upper-confidence-bound acquisition function, and the method selects parallel batches through heterotopic querying. It also supports a distinction between partial measurements and tasks. The paper frames heterotopic data as multiple correlated outputs or tasks that are not observed for every sample—for example, hardness measured for all alloys while tensile testing is performed only on a selected subset. Thus, the partial-observation aspect is task/property-level missingness rather than a clearly described sequence of intermediate measurements in a manufacturing process. The method uses deep multi-task Gaussian-process structure to transfer information across correlated properties and heterogeneous fidelity sources. Its demonstrated application is refractory high-entropy alloys for high-temperature applications. In the supplied pages, there is no indication that the study applies an alloy metal-additive-manufacturing directed acyclic graph (DAG), nor that it models an AM workflow as a DAG. The excerpt contains no substantive information about Hur and Lee, Chawla et al., or Comlek et al., so their cost-awareness, treatment of intermediate measurements versus tasks, and alloy metal-AM DAG status cannot be assessed from this source.

The excerpt identifies Hur and Lee’s framework as cost-aware through an uncertainty-gated, multi-fidelity measurement strategy. Low-cost, low-resolution measurements are used to predict selected high-cost, high-resolution measurements when the surrogate is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the agent requests the expensive characterization. Multiple partial intermediate inputs may also be combined when no single low-cost measurement is informative enough. The stated examples include hardness as a proxy for tensile strength and the combination of XRD, elemental composition, and CALPHAD calculations to reduce reliance on SEM/EBSD. Thus, the approach concerns measurement/characterization tasks within an experimental loop, rather than merely choosing experiments using a cost-aware acquisition function. The paper describes a metal additive-manufacturing self-driving laboratory being built around directed-energy-deposition printing, sample cutting, heat treatment, and X-ray, optical, and electron characterization. This is presented as an intended or ongoing integrated workflow, with evaluation planned for uncertainty calibration, hits per characterization cost, and time to target; the excerpt does not establish completed experimental results or a demonstrated production DAG. Alvi et al. is cited as prior work on cost-aware batch Bayesian optimization, but no details are provided here. Chawla et al. and Comlek et al. are not mentioned in the excerpt, so their treatment of costs, intermediate measurements, or applied Ti6Al4V/alloy workflows cannot be assessed from this source.

Vivek Chawla, Dayakar Penumadu, and Sergei Kalinin. Random combinatorial libraries and automated nanoindentation for high-throughput structural materials discovery. Communications Materials, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-026-01294-8, doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01294-8. This article has 1 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides evidence that Chawla et al. use a cost-aware Bayesian optimization workflow for random particle-based combinatorial libraries characterized by automated nanoindentation. Site selection maximizes an acquisition function normalized by travel and measurement costs; in the reported experiment, movement is negligible and the approximately five-second indentation measurement dominates cost. The strategy uses staged exploration and exploitation: beta is set to 2 initially, reduced to 1 after ten exploratory grids, and then to 0.1 with periodic increases for targeted exploration. The measured entities are discrete particles representing distinct points in a high-dimensional compositional space, and the workflow accounts for particle-edge failures through NaN values. Thus, the paper demonstrates cost-aware selection over individual characterization measurements rather than an explicitly described task-level manufacturing workflow. The conclusions state that the architecture can extend to processing-space exploration using inert markers and to synthesis pipelines, but this excerpt does not document an actually applied alloy-metal additive-manufacturing directed acyclic graph (DAG). It also does not provide information about Alvi et al., Hur and Lee, or Comlek et al., so their cost-awareness, treatment of partial intermediate measurements versus tasks, and additive-manufacturing applicability cannot be assessed from this excerpt.

5.1  Benchmarks and Comparison Metric

We evaluate the proposed Fast p-KGFN algorithm’s optimization performance against several baseline methods,
including standard Expected Improvement (EI) (Jones et al., 1998; Moˇckus, 1975), Knowledge Gradient (KG) (Frazier
et al., 2008; Wu and Frazier, 2016), and simple random sampling (Random), which do not utilize network structure.
Additionally, we compare to EIFN (Astudillo and Frazier, 2021a), Thompson Sampling for Function Networks (TSFN),
and Knowledge Gradient for Function Networks (KGFN), which exploit network structure but require full evaluations.
We also include the original p-KGFN algorithm, which supports partial evaluations and leverages network structure.

All algorithms start with the same uniformly sampled 2d + 1 initial observations, fully evaluated across the network,
where d is the network dimension. Algorithms proceed until the budget of 700 is exhausted. Performance is averaged
over 30 trials, each with different initial observations. We report at each iteration the average ground truth value yK(x∗n),
where x∗n ∈arg maxx∈X νn(x), with confidence intervals, as in Buathong et al. (2024). Though EI, KG and Random
do not leverage network structure in their sampling strategies, this metric is computed using a model that incorporates it.
We also report the CPU runtimes of each algorithm to validate our claim that the proposed algorithm is faster than the
original p-KGFN.

All algorithms are implemented using BoTorch (Balandat et al., 2020) in Python. Optimization settings, unless stated
otherwise, follow the implementations in Buathong et al. (2024). Code to reproduce our numerical experiments is
available at: https://github.com/frazier-lab/partial_kgfn.


6  Results


Figure 3 illustrates the performance of the proposed Fast p-KGFN algorithm compared to various benchmarks on the
AckMat (left), FreeSolv (middle), and Manu (right) problems. Among the evaluated methods, all except p-KGFN and
the proposed approach require full evaluations. Notably, only EIFN, KGFN, TSFN, p-KGFN, and the proposed method
incorporate the network structure into their sampling strategies. Furthermore, both p-KGFN and the proposed algorithm
support partial evaluations, enabling intermediate nodes to be evaluated at any input within their known ranges.

Overall, p-KGFN achieved the strongest optimization performance, closely followed by the proposed method. This
result is expected, as p-KGFN fully optimizes the acquisition function to select the most promising node-specific
candidate in each iteration. While the proposed method also supports partial evaluations, it reuses candidate points from
EIFN, which may slightly degrade candidate quality and introduce a minor performance trade-off. Nonetheless, the
proposed algorithm consistently outperforms the original EIFN, demonstrating the benefits of partial evaluations.

To further investigate the proposed method, we assess its sensitivity to varying evaluation costs. Specifically, we alter
the cost of evaluating the second node in AckMat and FreeSolv, considering three scenarios: (a) c1 = c2 = 1 (BO
budget = 50), (b) c1 = 1, c2 = 9 (BO budget = 150), and (c) c1 = 1, c2 = 49 (BO budget = 700). Figure 4 presents the
results. They show that the proposed algorithm behaves similarly to p-KGFN, with the benefits of partial evaluations
becoming more pronounced as the second node’s evaluation cost increases. This allows p-KGFN and the proposed
method to find better solutions more efficiently than other competitors. These findings confirm that despite slightly
lower-quality node-specific candidates, the proposed algorithm effectively leverages partial evaluations to achieve
strong optimization performance.

Beyond optimization quality, the proposed method substantially improves computational efficiency over p-KGFN.
Table 1 summarizes the average runtimes (across 30 trials on an 8-core CPU) for all cost settings, focusing on the
proposed algorithm, EIFN, and p-KGFN. The proposed method consistently achieved lower runtimes, with the most
notable speedup in FreeSolv under c1 = c2 = 1, where it attained a 16.03× improvement over p-KGFN. Appendix D
provides a full comparison of the Pareto fronts over acquisition runtime and final objective value for all methods.

In our ablation study on discrete point generation strategies, we find that excluding the maximizer of the current
posterior mean x∗n from the discrete set A significantly degrades the performance of Fast p-KGFN. The best results are

7  Conclusion

This work addresses Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (p-KGFN), a framework
designed for optimizing expensive objective functions structured as function networks, where each node can be queried
independently with varying evaluation costs. While p-KGFN finds better solutions with lower evaluation budgets than
traditional approaches, it suffers from high computational overhead due to its reliance on Monte Carlo simulations and
the need to solve individual acquisition function problems for node-specific candidate selection in each iteration.

To overcome these challenges, we propose a faster variant of p-KGFN that leverages the expected improvement for
function networks (EIFN) framework. Instead of solving separate acquisition problems for each node, the proposed
method generates a single candidate for the entire network using EIFN and combines it with simulated intermediate
outputs from the surrogate model to generate node-specific candidates. A cost-aware selection strategy then determines
which node and corresponding input candidate to evaluate at each iteration.

We evaluate the efficiency of the proposed method across multiple test problems. Our approach achieves competitive
optimization performance compared to p-KGFN while significantly reducing computational time, with the fastest
runtime improvement exceeding 16×.

Despite these advantages, our method has some limitations. It assumes that intermediate nodes can be evaluated at
any feasible input without requiring the outputs of parent nodes in advance, which may limit its applicability in more
constrained function network scenarios. Extending the method to handle upstream-downstream dependencies is an
important direction for future work.

3.3  Case Study 3: Manufacturing Process Fusion of Ti6Al4V Alloys


Titanium alloy (Ti6Al4V) has been at the forefront of aerospace applications due to its superior corrosion resistance,
strength, and toughness. The manufacturing of this alloy has evolved beyond the conventional casting process,
extending to additive and solid-state manufacturing processes such as Electron Beam Melting (EBM), Laser Powder
Bed Fusion (LPBF), and Friction Stir Welding (FSW). In the third and final case study, a multi-source data fusion
model across different manufacturing modalities, for the same alloy is demonstrated. Specifically, three thermally
driven manufacturing processes, EBM, LBPF, and FSW are selected as the data sources. A special characteristics of
this study is that there is a complete non-overlap in the input parameter space of the data sources, meaning that there is
no common parameter across sources. It is important to note that the complexity and cost of each source are open to
interpretation based on the modeling scenario. The fundamental question this work seeks to answer is whether learning
across different manufacturing modalities is possible for the same alloy through heterogeneous multi-source data fusion.

Heterogeneous Mapping  The initial step of the proposed framework involves identifying the mapping between EBM
and FSW to the LPBF input domain. A standalone GP model is trained on the LPBF data, which is then utilized in
the optimization framework to construct the A and b matrices. The transformations obtained for EBM and FSW to
LPBF are detailed through Equations 11 and 12. The transformation of EBM variables to the LPBF domain is primarily
influenced by the Focus Offset and Line Offset variables, with a minimal contribution from the Speed Factor. Intuitively,
this transformation aligns with the understanding of the amount of heat input into the system, which can significantly
influence the yield strength of the material. Specifically, this heat amount is primarily driven by Laser Power for LPBF
and a combination of Focus Offset and Line Offset for EBM. Both outputs are shifted by noticeable factors. The Laser

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18817-9, doi:10.1007/s00170-026-18817-9. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt provides evidence that de Sousa et al.’s AlSi10Mg L-DED study uses a sequential, multi-stage optimization workflow involving single beads, single layers, and multilayer geometries. The paper first establishes a stable single-bead processing window and evaluates spot size, laser power, travel speed, and powder feed rate. It then performs further single-layer optimization by adding hatch spacing and assesses energy-density effects on layer height, waviness, dilution, and deposition efficiency. For multilayer geometries, hatch spacing is selected using layer height, deposition efficiency, and densification, while contour-strategy effects are investigated. The excerpt explicitly states that processing parameters were optimized using regression and multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO). This supports characterizing the work as conventional parameter/process optimization conducted across successive geometric stages, rather than demonstrating an explicitly cost-aware acquisition policy based on a stage- or node-cost ratio. However, the supplied pages do not report the acquisition function, evaluation-cost model, budget allocation, or whether BO actively chooses among stages/nodes according to cost. They also contain no information about the Katagiri, Kavas, Taheri-Mousavi, Kiroriwal, or Kouraytem studies, nor enough information to establish process-structure-property-linked surrogate modeling beyond geometric and process-response optimization.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-026-18817-9, doi:10.1007/s00170-026-18817-9. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt indicates that the de Sousa et al. AlSi10Mg L-DED study performs ordinary multi-response parameter optimization rather than active acquisition based on a stage/node-cost ratio. The authors fit polynomial regression models to geometric properties, use feature selection and p-value-based term removal, and then apply desirability functions to predicted responses. The optimization evaluates a grid of L-DED parameter combinations, including laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing. Each combination is mapped to predicted dilution, average peak height, waviness, and deposition efficiency; individual desirabilities are combined through a geometric average to obtain a global desirability score. The selected solution is therefore the parameter set with the most desirable predicted properties under specified targets and limits, not a sequential Bayesian optimization policy explicitly balancing information gain, process cost, or acquisition-stage/node cost. The excerpt provides no information about Katagiri’s powder DEM BO, Kavas LPBF, the Taheri-Mousavi high-strength alloy AM paper, Kiroriwal’s 2026 manufacturing BO work, or Kouraytem’s 2021 review. Consequently, it cannot establish how those studies treat acquisition functions or process-structure-property-linked surrogates. It only supports classifying de Sousa’s described method as regression-based desirability/parameter optimization.

Bayesian optimization-based parameter identification for discrete element method simulation of consolidation and its application to powder spreading analysis. Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 9:383, Nov 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmmp9120383, doi:10.3390/jmmp9120383. This article has 1 citations.

Katagiri et al. (2025) is best classified as ordinary Bayesian-optimization-based parameter identification, rather than active acquisition explicitly formulated around a stage/node-cost ratio. The method calibrates two DEM parameters—the cohesion-related surface energy coefficient (k) and rolling resistance coefficient (µr)—against experimental void-ratio data from powder consolidation tests. Bayesian optimization is used to reduce the number of expensive DEM simulations required, but the excerpt does not describe an acquisition function or decision rule based on an explicit cost per optimization stage, node, or evaluation. The calibrated parameters reproduce consolidation behavior, yet their transfer to powder spreading produces excessively cohesive beds and poor layer uniformity. The authors attribute this to mechanical-scaling mismatch and a change from normal-force-dominated consolidation to shear-dominated spreading, concluding that spreading-relevant shear metrics and scaling should be included in calibration. Nothing in the provided excerpt establishes a process-structure-property linked surrogate, nor does it provide information about de Sousa AlSi10Mg L-DED, Kavas LPBF, Taheri-Mousavi’s high-strength-alloy AM work, Kiroriwal (2026), or Kouraytem (2021). Therefore, those papers cannot be classified from this excerpt; only Katagiri can be assessed, as conventional parameter optimization using BO for simulation-efficiency purposes.

Modeling process–structure–property relationships in metal additive manufacturing: a review on physics-driven versus data-driven approaches. Journal of Physics: Materials, 4:032002, Apr 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7639/abca7b, doi:10.1088/2515-7639/abca7b. This article has 229 citations.

This review provides a conceptual framework for distinguishing ordinary process-parameter optimization from models that explicitly represent process–structure–property (p-s-p) relationships. Metal AM uses many adjustable variables—including source power, scanning speed, scan strategy, layer thickness, and powder characteristics—and their interactions generate defects and heterogeneous microstructures that affect mechanical properties. Consequently, the literature frames numerical modeling and digital twins as ways to explore broad parameter spaces rather than relying on experimental trial and error. Physics-driven approaches use process and material physics to connect processing conditions to structure and properties, but they may require substantial computation and calibration. Data-driven approaches can predict complex behavior without traditional calibration, although interpretability and validation are limitations. The excerpt therefore supports treating a paper as p-s-p-linked when its surrogate or digital-twin model propagates information across process, resulting structure, and material/property variables. It does not, however, provide evidence about the specific de Sousa AlSi10Mg L-DED, Katagiri powder-DEM, Kavas LPBF, Taheri-Mousavi alloy-AM, or Kiroriwal 2026 studies, nor does it mention active acquisition or a stage/node-cost ratio. Those classifications require the methods and acquisition objectives reported in the respective papers.

Additively manufactured aluminum (Al) alloys with high strength have broad industrial applications. Strength promotion necessitates a high‐volume fraction of small, closely spaced precipitates to effectively impede dislocation motion. Here, it is shown that for certain compositions in the Al‐Er‐Zr‐Y‐Yb‐Ni alloy class, L12‐Al3M phases, the primary strength contributor, can initially precipitate as submicron‐scale (≈100 nm) metastable ternary phases under the rapid solidification of powder bed additive manufacturing; yet the subsequent coarsening‐resistant L12‐Al3M phases that precipitate during heat treatment remain at the nanometer scale, imparting high strength. This integrated computational‐experimental workflow shows the considerable potential to exploit rapid solidification in additive manufacturing to design alloys with commercially deployable properties.

Poompol Buathong and Peter I. Frazier. Fast bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations. ArXiv, Jun 2506. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2506.11456. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt directly locates the original 2024 Buathong et al. work in the references as “Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations,” published in the Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), pages 4752–4784. It also describes the 2025 Fast paper’s Manu test case. Manu is not presented as an actual alloy additive-manufacturing experiment or a real-world industrial dataset: it is explicitly a constructed manufacturing function network in which each function is sampled from a Gaussian-process prior with Matérn 5/2 kernels. The functions f1–f4 use length scales 0.631, 1, 1, and 3, respectively; all output scales are 0.631 except f4, whose output scale is 10. Intermediate outputs are constrained to y1 ∈ (−2, 2) and y2,y3 ∈ (−1, 1), while raw inputs x and x′ lie in (−1, 1). Node evaluation costs are c1=5, c2=10, c3=10, and c4=45. The optimization objective is to identify the optimal pair of raw-material inputs x and x′ maximizing final output y4. Thus, the scenario is a generic simulated manufacturing network designed to model heterogeneous process complexity and unequal evaluation costs, rather than a validated alloy-AM case.

{"answer": "## Assessment (literature searched through 6 October 2026)

**I did not find a non–Sterling G. Baird journal paper or preprint demonstrating the exact combination specified:** a cost-aware Bayesian optimizer that represents the *composition → powder atomization → laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) → microstructure → mechanical-property* route as a directed network of stage surrogates and adaptively decides whether to obtain another intermediate result or pay for a downstream measurement. This is a finding about the literature located, **not proof that no such publication exists**. Crucially, both the optimization method and nearly the entire physical alloy pipeline have substantial prior art; they should not be claimed as independently new. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000056)

### Closest precedents and what they actually demonstrate

| Work | Demonstrated contribution | Boundary relative to the proposed claim |
|---|---|---|
| **Astudillo and Frazier, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks* (2021).** | Models a directed network with separate Gaussian processes (GPs) and uses expected improvement informed by intermediate outputs. | The original general-network algorithm evaluates the **whole network** at each iteration; observing internal outputs is not itself a partial-evaluation policy. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000) |
| **Buathong *et al.*, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2023 preprint; ICML 2024).** | **Direct methodological precedent.** Its p-KGFN policy chooses a node and feasible input using expected improvement in the best posterior-mean solution **divided by that node’s evaluation cost**. In its principal setting, a downstream query uses *previously produced parent outputs*, so upstream dependencies are respected. | Its manufacturing example, **Manu-GP**, is a synthetic network sampled from GP priors, not an alloy-atomization/LPBF campaign; other demonstrations include molecular FreeSolv and pharmaceutical-product examples. Do not claim to invent cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000063) |
| **Buathong and Frazier, *Fast Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2025 preprint).** | Accelerates node-level, cost-aware p-KGFN selection, reporting up to **16.03-fold** lower acquisition runtime. | Its **Manu** case remains a simulated manufacturing network. Unlike the earlier paper’s main feasible-input setting, this fast variant assumes a node can be queried at a feasible input **without first obtaining its parent outputs**; the authors identify physically constrained dependencies as future work. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000063) |
| **Torresi and Friederich, *Multi-stage Bayesian optimisation for dynamic decision-making in self-driving labs* (*Digital Discovery*, 2026).** | A particularly close **cascade-GP and partial-workflow** analogue: an inventory preserves intermediate samples; nested expected improvement chooses between starting samples and advancing existing ones. The framework permits stage-cost weighting. It is tested on synthetic cascades and retrospective molecular-property datasets, including simulated-versus-experimental hydration free energy. | **Not metal AM.** Moreover, although heterogeneous costs are tested, the authors report using **uniform stage costs in their principal experiments** because explicit cost weighting performed worse; their heterogeneous-cost benefit can arise from resumable sampling without putting cost into the acquisition. It should not be described unqualifiedly as an empirical demonstration of information-per-unit-cost selection in alloys. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) |
| **Taheri-Mousavi *et al.*, 2024 preprint and *Advanced Materials* article (2026), DOI 10.1002/adma.202509507.** | **Closest physical-pipeline precedent.** CALPHAD/ICME-informed **composition BO** led to a custom Al alloy; the authors screened compositions and printability, **ultrasonically atomized powder**, optimized LPBF settings, examined microstructure, and performed hardness and tensile testing. The journal abstract reports **395 MPa** tensile strength after aging. | Its BO selects alloy compositions against simulated design metrics; subsequent screening, powder production, printing and testing are **not reported as competing costed nodes selected by a BOFN partial-evaluation acquisition**. Thus the *integrated composition-to-property AM route* has precedent, even if the proposed **adaptive stage-selection rule applied across it** has not been located. (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057) |
| **Alvi *et al.*, *npj Computational Materials* (2026).** | Cost-aware, batch deep-GP BO chooses among **unequally costly property/information-source queries** for refractory high-entropy-alloy design; not every alloy receives every measurement. | The reported alloy case is **in silico** and concerns heterogeneous property tasks, **not sequential atomization → LPBF → microstructure → testing nodes**. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032) |
| **Hur and Lee, *Compressing the Validation Bottleneck* (2026 preprint).** | Proposes a cost-aware metal-AM measurement agent that could use hardness instead of tensile testing, or X-ray/composition/CALPHAD instead of more expensive characterization, requesting the latter when prediction uncertainty is high. | Calls the DED-based metal-AM laboratory one the authors **“are building”** and describes evaluation in the future tense; it does **not establish a completed, experimentally demonstrated BOFN/LPBF pipeline**. It nevertheless makes broad claims about *first cost-aware intermediate-versus-final measurement decisions in metal AM* especially risky. (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000047) |
| **de Sousa *et al.*, *International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology* (2026); Comlek *et al.*, *Journal of Mechanical Design* (2025).** | De Sousa combines single-bead, single-layer and multilayer experiments with GP/multiobjective optimization for **AlSi10Mg laser directed-energy deposition**. Comlek fuses previously published **LPBF, electron-beam-melting and welding** data with a source-aware GP to predict Ti–6Al–4V yield strength. | Respectively, a staged **process-parameter** study rather than acquisition among costed pipeline nodes, and **predictive multi-source GP fusion** rather than sequential experimental BO. Neither is the specified LPBF alloy-production BOFN. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000046) |

Additional single-stage precedents are Tamura *et al.*’s 2021 BO of **Ni–Co superalloy gas-atomization parameters** and Kavas *et al.*’s 2025 preprint on BO-tuned **LPBF feedback control**. They optimize different parts of the proposed route, not a shared cost-aware, composition-to-mechanical-property function network. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000053)

### Is “applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys” defensible?

**Not as written.** It leaves the distinguishing algorithmic feature unstated and can be read as claiming priority for applying BO to an integrated alloy-AM pipeline—despite the Taheri-Mousavi composition-to-powder-to-LPBF-to-property study—or for partial-evaluation, cost-aware network BO, which Buathong *et al.* had already developed. If the intended contribution is a *new application of an existing acquisition principle* to an experimentally realized, physically constrained **alloy LPBF process network**, a carefully delimited, qualified priority claim remains **plausible on the literature found**, but cannot be guaranteed by a search. It is important to specify whether intermediate queries are genuinely feasible given parent outputs and whether stage costs actually affect the next-evaluation decisions; merely recording intermediate observations, running inexpensive simulations before expensive tests, or using chained GPs is insufficient. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000045)

**Safer wording:** “To our knowledge, this is the first *demonstrated application of cost-aware Bayesian optimization of a partially evaluable function network* to an integrated **metal-alloy composition–powder-production–LPBF–microstructure–mechanical-property workflow**, in which the optimizer adaptively selects feasible intermediate or downstream evaluations under stage-dependent costs.” **Use “demonstrated” and list every stage only if the reported study actually executes or validates those stages and shows adaptive choices between them**; otherwise say “we propose a framework for…” and name only the stages implemented. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000047)"}

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts Astudillo and Frazier’s structured-objective Bayesian optimisation with later function-network and multi-stage approaches. BOFN models a directed acyclic graph in which each node is represented by an independent Gaussian process and uses a Monte Carlo acquisition function, but the standard formulation evaluates the full network at every iteration. This limits selective sub-graph sampling and creates computational overhead from nested Monte Carlo estimators and repeated acquisition optimisation. Partially observable knowledge-gradient extensions permit selective intermediate-node evaluation, although the excerpt notes that such approaches may assume intermediate nodes can be queried independently of upstream stages, which is often unrealistic in laboratory workflows. Torresi and Friederich’s MSBO instead supports causally feasible partial cascade evaluations, preserves partially processed samples through a state-saving inventory, and uses a nested, stage-aware acquisition function. Its design explicitly addresses sequential experimental costs and dynamic workflow adaptation. The reported demonstrations are synthetic multi-stage functions and a data-trained solar-cell simulator. The excerpt contains no evidence of a metal-alloy additive-manufacturing application. Other relevant works named here include cascade Bayesian optimisation, BOFN, partially observable knowledge-gradient methods, multi-fidelity BO, Hyperband, BOHB, Freeze–Thaw BO, and Kusakawa et al.’s cascade-process method; however, the excerpt does not provide enough detail to rank their applications or compare their explicit cost models fully.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Astudillo and Frazier’s Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), in which an objective is produced by a directed acyclic network of time-consuming functions. Standard BO models only the final objective output and ignores intermediate-node observations, whereas BOFN assigns distinct Gaussian processes to network nodes and recursively incorporates observations of internal outputs into a generally non-Gaussian posterior over the final objective. Its explicit acquisition function is expected improvement under that implied posterior; because the posterior is non-Gaussian, expected improvement is maximized using sample average approximation. The vaccine-manufacturing example illustrates a full sequential network evaluation: cell culture, purification, and formulation, with the goal of maximizing final protein yield. Intermediate outputs can diagnose which stage or input is responsible for poor performance and may reduce the effective search dimension. The excerpt emphasizes query efficiency, asymptotic consistency, and avoiding dense exploration. It does not describe selective evaluation of only a subset of nodes, node-specific acquisition decisions, or explicit differentiated costs for partial evaluations; thus those aspects cannot be attributed to this excerpt. Applications mentioned include reinforcement-learning policy search, complex-system simulation, physics-model calibration, manufacturing, robotics, and epidemiology/COVID-19. No metal-alloy additive-manufacturing application is identified in the provided pages, and Torresi and Friederich’s multi-stage dynamic-decision method is not covered here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Buathong et al. (arXiv:2311.02146) as a Bayesian-optimization method for function networks in which evaluations may be partial rather than full-network. Its action is to select an individual node and a corresponding input for evaluation, then use the resulting information to choose inputs to subsequent nodes; the introduction explicitly contrasts this with evaluating the full network at every iteration. The excerpt lists manufacturing, epidemic-model calibration, machine-learning pipeline optimization, and robotic control as application domains, and says experiments cover synthetic and real-world problems. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the 2025 Buathong–Frazier Fast p-KGFN work, but does not provide the bibliographic publication venue/date details for the earlier arXiv:2311.02146 paper, nor any alloy-additive-manufacturing experiment. It characterizes function-network optimization using a DAG of constituent functions and explains that partial evaluations query only selected nodes rather than necessarily evaluating the entire objective. contexts.context: Tamura et al. (2021) is a strong primary study relevant to composition/material-processing optimization, but the excerpt describes powder gas atomization rather than metal additive manufacturing or LPBF itself. The study applies expert-free Bayesian optimization, beginning with only three experimental data sets and using three optimization cycles to select atomization parameters for a Ni-Co-based superalloy intended for turbine-disk applications. The variables explicitly optimized were melt temperature and gas pressure. The principal objective was to increase the yield of fine powder below 53 μm, a size range required after sieving to remove large inclusions. The reported outcome was a 77.85% yield, compared with the typical 10–30%, and an approximately 72% reduction in manufacturing cost relative to commercial powder. The broader quality requirements included low oxygen, high circularity, and low microsegregation, although the excerpt does not establish that all were jointly optimized by the Bayesian model. This work therefore supports the powder-atomization component of the requested comparison, but it does not report LPBF builds, sequential bead/layer/multilayer experiments, or microstructure/mechanical testing as the optimization target in the supplied pages. No cost-aware node choice in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is described; cost appears only as a resulting economic benefit, not as an explicit DAG decision criterion.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024), a relevant non-Baird alloy-design study using Bayesian optimization (BO) coupled to ICME/CALPHAD-style simulations. The primary objective was minimizing a coarsening metric while constraining Er and Zr contents; the design was reduced to Er–Zr space and then Ni was optimized using Scheil solidification predictions to promote a metastable ternary Al23Ni6M4 reservoir and subsequent L12 precipitation. The study compared direct ICME evaluations, a neural-network surrogate, and particle-swarm optimization. The explicit computational action/cost choice was to spend 40 simulated composition–coarsening samples to train the NN surrogate, after which BO converged with 100 surrogate evaluations; direct BO/ICME required approximately 80 samples. The selected composition achieved a coarsening metric 3.5 times lower than the benchmark. Experimental validation proceeded through induction melting and laser scanning for printability, followed by hardness testing before and after aging. The work then covered the full materials route more closely than a simulation-only study: custom powder was produced by ultrasonic atomization, LPBF parameters were optimized for density, and printed samples were characterized for cracking, grain structure, and hardness. However, the excerpt does not establish cost-aware multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, multi-source active learning, process–structure–property linked Gaussian processes, or comparisons among intermediate and expensive measurements. It is also a 2024 preprint, not a 2025–2026 source.

contexts.context: Alvi et al. present a cost-aware, batch heterotopic deep Gaussian process Bayesian optimization framework for multi-objective materials discovery. The approach allocates queries across property-evaluation tasks with unequal costs: expensive properties such as thermal conductivity and solidus temperature receive relatively few evaluations, while cheaper measurements—including density, Pugh ratio, hardness, and BCC phase fraction—are sampled more heavily. These are partial or auxiliary property measurements rather than intermediate manufacturing-process states; the model uses learned inter-task correlations so abundant inexpensive data can improve predictions for expensive properties. The demonstrated materials case is a seven-dimensional Ti–Ta–V–W–Cr–Fe–Hf refractory high-entropy-alloy composition space, optimizing solidus temperature, thermal conductivity, yield strength, BCC phase fraction, and density. The study is explicitly an in-silico CALPHAD-based campaign, not an experimental alloy metal-additive-manufacturing deployment. The authors identify future joint chemistry–process optimization—such as temperature profiles, cooling rates, mechanical working parameters, and synthesis routes—as a needed extension. Thus, this excerpt supports classification as cost-aware and multi-task/heterotopic, but does not document an actually applied additive-manufacturing DAG or an experimental process DAG.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Hur and Lee’s framework as cost-aware through an uncertainty-gated, multi-fidelity measurement strategy. Low-cost, low-resolution measurements are used to predict selected high-cost, high-resolution measurements when the surrogate is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the agent requests the expensive characterization. Multiple partial intermediate inputs may also be combined when no single low-cost measurement is informative enough. The stated examples include hardness as a proxy for tensile strength and the combination of XRD, elemental composition, and CALPHAD calculations to reduce reliance on SEM/EBSD. Thus, the approach concerns measurement/characterization tasks within an experimental loop, rather than merely choosing experiments using a cost-aware acquisition function. The paper describes a metal additive-manufacturing self-driving laboratory being built around directed-energy-deposition printing, sample cutting, heat treatment, and X-ray, optical, and electron characterization. This is presented as an intended or ongoing integrated workflow, with evaluation planned for uncertainty calibration, hits per characterization cost, and time to target; the excerpt does not establish completed experimental results or a demonstrated production DAG. Alvi et al. is cited as prior work on cost-aware batch Bayesian optimization, but no details are provided here. Chawla et al. and Comlek et al. are not mentioned in the excerpt, so their treatment of costs, intermediate measurements, or applied Ti6Al4V/alloy workflows cannot be assessed from this source.

The surrogate uncertainty is low, the agent uses the prediction from the low-cost measurement result; when the uncertainty is high, the agent requests the high-cost measurement

We will evaluate surrogate accuracy and uncertainty calibration on held-out measurements, on-target hits per characterization cost relative to measuring everything, and wall-clock time to reach a target specification.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a heterogeneous multi-source latent-variable Gaussian process (LVGP), not cost-aware BOFN or adaptive partial evaluation. It transfers information among sources with differing parameterizations, complexity, and fidelity. In the ellipsoidal-void study, 2DE (273 training/117 testing; cheapest elastic analysis), 3DE (182/77; elastic), and 3DER (10/40; costlier plastic analysis) predict maximum von Mises stress. contexts.context:
The excerpt defines p-KGFN, a cost-aware knowledge-gradient method for function networks with partial evaluations. Independent Gaussian processes model nodes; previously generated parent outputs determine feasible downstream inputs. For node \(k\), acquisition is
\[
\alpha_{n,k}(z_k)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{y_k}[\nu^*_{n+1}]-\nu^*_n}{c_k(z_k)},
\]
and the next node/input maximizes this value. Intermediate outputs are reusable, enabling selective evaluation rather than full-network runs. A two-stage example uses costs \(c_1=1\), \(c_2=49\), and a budget of 150; p-KGFN outperforms full-evaluation EIFN conceptually. No metals additive-manufacturing application appears in this excerpt.

contexts.context: A 2026 *Digital Discovery* paper presents MSBO (multi-stage Bayesian optimization) for cascade processes, explicitly modeling dependent stages with a “cascade of GPs.” Each stage follows \(h_i=f_i(x_i,h_{i-1})+\epsilon_i^p\), while observations may be partial: \(m_i=M_i h_i+\epsilon_i^m\). An inventory stores partially processed samples, enabling processing to stop, resume, and “select which sub-process to sample next based on acquisition function values.” Monte Carlo propagates uncertainty through nonlinear stages, and nested acquisition functions address heterogeneous computational costs. The excerpt frames applications broadly (chemical manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, material processing), but does not identify a metal-alloy AM demonstration.

contexts.context: A 2026 *Digital Discovery* paper presents “MSBO,” a nested/cascade BO framework using independent Gaussian processes for sequential stages. Intermediate predictive distributions propagate uncertainty downstream via Monte Carlo (Sobol \(S=256\)); acquisition is recursively defined from final-stage EI, and the next stage is selected by \(\arg\max_i a_i/c_i\), explicitly accounting for heterogeneous costs. It supports Markovian or residual dependencies and partially observed outputs. Experiments cover synthetic functions and molecular-property prediction, not the specified metal-alloy additive-manufacturing pipeline. Thus it is a close methodological analogue, but does not itself establish AM application.

contexts.context: Buathong et al.’s BOFN paper (arXiv:2311.02146v2; authors include Cornell, Caltech, Meta) introduces partial evaluations for directed function networks. Its cost-aware knowledge-gradient method, p-KGFN, “iteratively selects a node… and a corresponding input,” using intermediate outputs and heterogeneous node costs to minimize simple regret. The authors state prior BOFN methods evaluated the full network and that their acquisition function is “the first” for cost-aware optimization of a broad class of function networks.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates “Fast p-KGFN,” a cost-aware BOFN method allowing independent intermediate-node queries and selecting node/input by cost-aware acquisition. Experiments use synthetic AckMat and FreeSolv networks plus “Manu,” with costs up to \(c_4=45\), budget 700, and 30 trials—not a metal-AM pipeline. Crucially, it assumes intermediate nodes are evaluable without parent outputs; handling upstream/downstream dependencies is identified as future work.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that de Sousa et al.’s AlSi10Mg L-DED study uses a sequential, multi-stage optimization workflow involving single beads, single layers, and multilayer geometries. The paper first establishes a stable single-bead processing window and evaluates spot size, laser power, travel speed, and powder feed rate. It then performs further single-layer optimization by adding hatch spacing and assesses energy-density effects on layer height, waviness, dilution, and deposition efficiency. For multilayer geometries, hatch spacing is selected using layer height, deposition efficiency, and densification, while contour-strategy effects are investigated. The excerpt explicitly states that processing parameters were optimized using regression and multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO). This supports characterizing the work as conventional parameter/process optimization conducted across successive geometric stages, rather than demonstrating an explicitly cost-aware acquisition policy based on a stage- or node-cost ratio. However, the supplied pages do not report the acquisition function, evaluation-cost model, budget allocation, or whether BO actively chooses among stages/nodes according to cost. They also contain no information about the Katagiri, Kavas, Taheri-Mousavi, Kiroriwal, or Kouraytem studies, nor enough information to establish process-structure-property-linked surrogate modeling beyond geometric and process-response optimization.

contexts.context: The Kavas et al. LPBF paper concerns Bayesian-optimization-based tuning of an in-layer PI controller, rather than active acquisition framed as a stage/node-cost-ratio problem. BO selects or adjusts controller parameters, specifically PI gains, using the repetitive layer-to-layer structure of LPBF. It evaluates two modes: online tuning during the printing process and offline tuning in a representative experimental setup, such as laser exposure on a bare metal plate. The resulting controllers are tested on overheating-prone wedge geometries, where both tuning approaches reduce overheating relative to uncontrolled specimens. The study therefore fits ordinary controller-parameter optimization, albeit with sequential, sample-efficient Bayesian optimization and an online/offline experimental design. The excerpt does not describe process-structure-property-linked surrogate models, nor does it establish links among process parameters, microstructure, and properties as the primary optimization framework. It does mention microstructural analysis of printed parts and identifies lack-of-fusion-type porosity caused by insufficient laser power, but this is presented as an observed consequence and limitation of controller tuning rather than as a coupled surrogate model. No information is provided here about de Sousa, Katagiri, Taheri-Mousavi, Kiroriwal, or Kouraytem, so their classifications cannot be inferred from this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that the de Sousa et al. AlSi10Mg L-DED study performs ordinary multi-response parameter optimization rather than active acquisition based on a stage/node-cost ratio. The authors fit polynomial regression models to geometric properties, use feature selection and p-value-based term removal, and then apply desirability functions to predicted responses. The optimization evaluates a grid of L-DED parameter combinations, including laser power, travel speed, and hatch spacing. Each combination is mapped to predicted dilution, average peak height, waviness, and deposition efficiency; individual desirabilities are combined through a geometric average to obtain a global desirability score. The selected solution is therefore the parameter set with the most desirable predicted properties under specified targets and limits, not a sequential Bayesian optimization policy explicitly balancing information gain, process cost, or acquisition-stage/node cost. The excerpt provides no information about Katagiri’s powder DEM BO, Kavas LPBF, the Taheri-Mousavi high-strength alloy AM paper, Kiroriwal’s 2026 manufacturing BO work, or Kouraytem’s 2021 review. Consequently, it cannot establish how those studies treat acquisition functions or process-structure-property-linked surrogates. It only supports classifying de Sousa’s described method as regression-based desirability/parameter optimization.

contexts.context: Katagiri et al. (2025) is best classified as ordinary Bayesian-optimization-based parameter identification, rather than active acquisition explicitly formulated around a stage/node-cost ratio. The method calibrates two DEM parameters—the cohesion-related surface energy coefficient (k) and rolling resistance coefficient (µr)—against experimental void-ratio data from powder consolidation tests. Bayesian optimization is used to reduce the number of expensive DEM simulations required, but the excerpt does not describe an acquisition function or decision rule based on an explicit cost per optimization stage, node, or evaluation. The calibrated parameters reproduce consolidation behavior, yet their transfer to powder spreading produces excessively cohesive beds and poor layer uniformity. The authors attribute this to mechanical-scaling mismatch and a change from normal-force-dominated consolidation to shear-dominated spreading, concluding that spreading-relevant shear metrics and scaling should be included in calibration. contexts.context: This review provides a conceptual framework for distinguishing ordinary process-parameter optimization from models that explicitly represent process–structure–property (p-s-p) relationships. Metal AM uses many adjustable variables—including source power, scanning speed, scan strategy, layer thickness, and powder characteristics—and their interactions generate defects and heterogeneous microstructures that affect mechanical properties. Consequently, the literature frames numerical modeling and digital twins as ways to explore broad parameter spaces rather than relying on experimental trial and error. Physics-driven approaches use process and material physics to connect processing conditions to structure and properties, but they may require substantial computation and calibration. Data-driven approaches can predict complex behavior without traditional calibration, although interpretability and validation are limitations. The excerpt therefore supports treating a paper as p-s-p-linked when its surrogate or digital-twin model propagates information across process, resulting structure, and material/property variables. contexts.context: The excerpt directly locates the original 2024 Buathong et al. work in the references as “Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations,” published in the Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), pages 4752–4784. It also describes the 2025 Fast paper’s Manu test case. Manu is not presented as an actual alloy additive-manufacturing experiment or a real-world industrial dataset: it is explicitly a constructed manufacturing function network in which each function is sampled from a Gaussian-process prior with Matérn 5/2 kernels. The functions f1–f4 use length scales 0.631, 1, 1, and 3, respectively; all output scales are 0.631 except f4, whose output scale is 10. Intermediate outputs are constrained to y1 ∈ (−2, 2) and y2,y3 ∈ (−1, 1), while raw inputs x and x′ lie in (−1, 1). Node evaluation costs are c1=5, c2=10, c3=10, and c4=45. The optimization objective is to identify the optimal pair of raw-material inputs x and x′ maximizing final output y4. Thus, the scenario is a generic simulated manufacturing network designed to model heterogeneous process complexity and unequal evaluation costs, rather than a validated alloy-AM case.

contexts.context: A 2026 *Digital Discovery* paper presents “MSBO,” a nested optimization framework for sequential/cascade processes. It models each stage with independent GPs, using Markovian inputs \([x_i,m_{i-1}]\) or residual inputs \([x_i,x_{i-1},m_{i-1}]\), and recursively propagates intermediate uncertainty via Monte Carlo (\(S=256\)). It selects among stages using cost-weighted acquisition, \(\arg\max_{i,x_i} a_i/c_i\), balancing continuation of existing samples against starting new ones. Demonstrations cover synthetic functions and molecular-property prediction—not metal-alloy additive manufacturing.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone applied cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks
(BOFN) with partial evaluations - i.e., an optimizer that models a multi-stage
pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models and chooses which
intermediate node (e.g., a cheap thermodynamic simulation or proxy experiment
vs. an expensive final property measurement) to evaluate next based on
information gained per unit cost - to an additive manufacturing pipeline for
metal alloys (composition -> powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion ->
microstructure -> mechanical property)? Consider both journal papers and
preprints, with emphasis on anything from 2025-2026, and include close
analogues (multi-stage / cascade BO, multi-fidelity BO with intermediate
process outputs, process-structure-property chained Gaussian processes) in
metals AM, alloy design, or other materials-manufacturing pipelines. Exclude
publications by Sterling G. Baird. State clearly whether the claim "applied
for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys"
is still defensible, and suggest a safer wording if not.


No. ## Assessment (literature searched through 6 October 2026)

**I did not find a non–Sterling G. Baird journal paper or preprint demonstrating the exact combination specified:** a cost-aware Bayesian optimizer that represents the *composition → powder atomization → laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) → microstructure → mechanical-property* route as a directed network of stage surrogates and adaptively decides whether to obtain another intermediate result or pay for a downstream measurement. This is a finding about the literature located, **not proof that no such publication exists**. Crucially, both the optimization method and nearly the entire physical alloy pipeline have substantial prior art; they should not be claimed as independently new. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12)

### Closest precedents and what they actually demonstrate

| Work | Demonstrated contribution | Boundary relative to the proposed claim |
|---|---|---|
| **Astudillo and Frazier, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks* (2021).** | Models a directed network with separate Gaussian processes (GPs) and uses expected improvement informed by intermediate outputs. | The original general-network algorithm evaluates the **whole network** at each iteration; observing internal outputs is not itself a partial-evaluation policy. (astudillo2021bayesianoptimizationof pages 1-2, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 2-3) |
| **Buathong *et al.*, *Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2023 preprint; ICML 2024).** | **Direct methodological precedent.** Its p-KGFN policy chooses a node and feasible input using expected improvement in the best posterior-mean solution **divided by that node’s evaluation cost**. In its principal setting, a downstream query uses *previously produced parent outputs*, so upstream dependencies are respected. | Its manufacturing example, **Manu-GP**, is a synthetic network sampled from GP priors, not an alloy-atomization/LPBF campaign; other demonstrations include molecular FreeSolv and pharmaceutical-product examples. Do not claim to invent cost-aware BOFN with partial evaluations. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 7-8, buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 8-9, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 9-11) |
| **Buathong and Frazier, *Fast Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations* (2025 preprint).** | Accelerates node-level, cost-aware p-KGFN selection, reporting up to **16.03-fold** lower acquisition runtime. | Its **Manu** case remains a simulated manufacturing network. Unlike the earlier paper’s main feasible-input setting, this fast variant assumes a node can be queried at a feasible input **without first obtaining its parent outputs**; the authors identify physically constrained dependencies as future work. (buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 8-9, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 9-11) |
| **Torresi and Friederich, *Multi-stage Bayesian optimisation for dynamic decision-making in self-driving labs* (*Digital Discovery*, 2026).** | A particularly close **cascade-GP and partial-workflow** analogue: an inventory preserves intermediate samples; nested expected improvement chooses between starting samples and advancing existing ones. The framework permits stage-cost weighting. It is tested on synthetic cascades and retrospective molecular-property datasets, including simulated-versus-experimental hydration free energy. | **Not metal AM.** Moreover, although heterogeneous costs are tested, the authors report using **uniform stage costs in their principal experiments** because explicit cost weighting performed worse; their heterogeneous-cost benefit can arise from resumable sampling without putting cost into the acquisition. It should not be described unqualifiedly as an empirical demonstration of information-per-unit-cost selection in alloys. (torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 5-6, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 6-7, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 7-10, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 10-12) |
| **Taheri-Mousavi *et al.*, 2024 preprint and *Advanced Materials* article (2026), DOI 10.1002/adma.202509507.** | **Closest physical-pipeline precedent.** CALPHAD/ICME-informed **composition BO** led to a custom Al alloy; the authors screened compositions and printability, **ultrasonically atomized powder**, optimized LPBF settings, examined microstructure, and performed hardness and tensile testing. The journal abstract reports **395 MPa** tensile strength after aging. | Its BO selects alloy compositions against simulated design metrics; subsequent screening, powder production, printing and testing are **not reported as competing costed nodes selected by a BOFN partial-evaluation acquisition**. Thus the *integrated composition-to-property AM route* has precedent, even if the proposed **adaptive stage-selection rule applied across it** has not been located. (taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 7-9, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 9-12, taheri‐mousavi2026additivelymanufacturablehigh‐strength pages 1-4) |
| **Alvi *et al.*, *npj Computational Materials* (2026).** | Cost-aware, batch deep-GP BO chooses among **unequally costly property/information-source queries** for refractory high-entropy-alloy design; not every alloy receives every measurement. | The reported alloy case is **in silico** and concerns heterogeneous property tasks, **not sequential atomization → LPBF → microstructure → testing nodes**. (alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 14-16, alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 2-4, alvi2026deepgaussianprocessbased pages 1-2) |
| **Hur and Lee, *Compressing the Validation Bottleneck* (2026 preprint).** | Proposes a cost-aware metal-AM measurement agent that could use hardness instead of tensile testing, or X-ray/composition/CALPHAD instead of more expensive characterization, requesting the latter when prediction uncertainty is high. | Calls the DED-based metal-AM laboratory one the authors **“are building”** and describes evaluation in the future tense; it does **not establish a completed, experimentally demonstrated BOFN/LPBF pipeline**. It nevertheless makes broad claims about *first cost-aware intermediate-versus-final measurement decisions in metal AM* especially risky. (hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 1-2, hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 2-4) |
| **de Sousa *et al.*, *International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology* (2026); Comlek *et al.*, *Journal of Mechanical Design* (2025).** | De Sousa combines single-bead, single-layer and multilayer experiments with GP/multiobjective optimization for **AlSi10Mg laser directed-energy deposition**. Comlek fuses previously published **LPBF, electron-beam-melting and welding** data with a source-aware GP to predict Ti–6Al–4V yield strength. | Respectively, a staged **process-parameter** study rather than acquisition among costed pipeline nodes, and **predictive multi-source GP fusion** rather than sequential experimental BO. Neither is the specified LPBF alloy-production BOFN. (sousa2026gaussianprocessregression pages 1-2, sousa2026gaussianprocessregression pages 15-17, comlek2025heterogeneousmultisourcedata pages 13-17) |

Additional single-stage precedents are Tamura *et al.*’s 2021 BO of **Ni–Co superalloy gas-atomization parameters** and Kavas *et al.*’s 2025 preprint on BO-tuned **LPBF feedback control**. They optimize different parts of the proposed route, not a shared cost-aware, composition-to-mechanical-property function network. (tamura2021machinelearningdrivenoptimization pages 1-5, kavas2025insitucontrollerautotuning pages 1-3)

### Is “applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys” defensible?

**Not as written.** It leaves the distinguishing algorithmic feature unstated and can be read as claiming priority for applying BO to an integrated alloy-AM pipeline—despite the Taheri-Mousavi composition-to-powder-to-LPBF-to-property study—or for partial-evaluation, cost-aware network BO, which Buathong *et al.* had already developed. If the intended contribution is a *new application of an existing acquisition principle* to an experimentally realized, physically constrained **alloy LPBF process network**, a carefully delimited, qualified priority claim remains **plausible on the literature found**, but cannot be guaranteed by a search. It is important to specify whether intermediate queries are genuinely feasible given parent outputs and whether stage costs actually affect the next-evaluation decisions; merely recording intermediate observations, running inexpensive simulations before expensive tests, or using chained GPs is insufficient. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, torresi2026multistagebayesianoptimisation pages 6-7, buathong2506fastbayesianoptimization pages 8-9)

**Safer wording:** “To our knowledge, this is the first *demonstrated application of cost-aware Bayesian optimization of a partially evaluable function network* to an integrated **metal-alloy composition–powder-production–LPBF–microstructure–mechanical-property workflow**, in which the optimizer adaptively selects feasible intermediate or downstream evaluations under stage-dependent costs.” **Use “demonstrated” and list every stage only if the reported study actually executes or validates those stages and shows adaptive choices between them**; otherwise say “we propose a framework for…” and name only the stages implemented. (buathong2023bayesianoptimizationof pages 3-4, taherimousavi2024additivelymanufacturablehighstrength pages 9-12, hur2607compressingthevalidation pages 2-4)

info.query:
Has anyone applied cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks
(BOFN) with partial evaluations - i.e., an optimizer that models a multi-stage
pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models and chooses which
intermediate node (e.g., a cheap thermodynamic simulation or proxy experiment
vs. an expensive final property measurement) to evaluate next based on
information gained per unit cost - to an additive manufacturing pipeline for
metal alloys (composition -> powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion ->
microstructure -> mechanical property)? Consider both journal papers and
preprints, with emphasis on anything from 2025-2026, and include close
analogues (multi-stage / cascade BO, multi-fidelity BO with intermediate
process outputs, process-structure-property chained Gaussian processes) in
metals AM, alloy design, or other materials-manufacturing pipelines. Exclude
publications by Sterling G. Baird. State clearly whether the claim "applied
for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys"
is still defensible, and suggest a safer wording if not.
